Glossary — phases, archetypes, 5-axis, and terms
Phase I / II / III — Activation horizon: Immediate revenue 0–18 mo · Structured strategy 18–36 mo · Enterprise / district transformation 36 mo+.
Multi-phase site — Most sites activate across more than one phase. They carry a chip per phase and surface in every phase tab they belong to; the primary phase is highlighted in the rollup.
Archetype — Strategic role — one of 6: Cloverleaf stacked-revenue · District-infrastructure platform · Campus-optimization prototype · Small infill housing platform · Strategic activation w/ optionality · Solar-overlay-and-go.
5-axis constraint — Legal / Operational / Community / Political / Market, each rated for surmountability: S surmountable, C conditional, H hard.
Cluster — The Wilmington Cluster moves as one district platform; it appears in Phase I (parking/solar) and Phase III (TOD). Sub-cards carry a Standalone-capable badge where they can activate alone.
Revenue pathway — One of the five sourced revenue categories (solar, EV, telecom, truck parking, outdoor advertising) plus the Cloverleaf integration model. Site cards link to the matching pathway.
Decision line — Each card leads with the next action and the legal authority/gate so a reviewer can route it.
Ground Lease — State keeps the land; developer builds and pays recurring rent.
Opportunity Zone (OZ) — Federal capital-gains incentive tract.
DDD — Wilmington Downtown Development District incentive area.
Confidence — High / Medium / Indicative — how firmly numbers and path are anchored.
Illustrative / Planning-level — Estimate, not a formal appraisal or underwriting. Solar revenue is under active refinement against Delaware PSC-filed tariff + REPSA data.
Two "EO 18"s — Delaware has two Executive Order 18s: Markell's 2010 energy order (13 DE Reg 1228, on-site PV authority) and Meyer's Feb 2026 Permitting Accelerator. Both are cited; the shared number is coincidental.
Section 1

Executive Findings

What Delaware is building

Enterprise Public Asset Optimization

Delaware’s State portfolio is one of the State’s most underutilized revenue assets. Across highway corridors, downtown Wilmington, and operational campuses, the State controls land that can support recurring revenue from solar, EV charging, telecommunications, truck parking, ground leases, and mixed-use redevelopment — without selling the land, raising taxes, or fronting capital. Every activation is a license to a private operator. The State keeps the underlying asset and collects the recurring stream.

We started with everything the State owns and narrowed to what can move now.

Each step is a filter, not a loss: 1,000+ State-controlled parcels → ~195 screened → 14 priority projects, together holding 38 parcels and 61 distinct revenue surfaces. Fourteen projects beat twenty scattered parcels because three moves — clustering, multi-phase activations, and cloverleaf stacking — pack more value per site. Tier is not Phase. Tier is how ready a site is to move (move-first → federally gated). Phase is the kind of activation work and its time-to-revenue. Every site has one tier and can run across more than one phase.

Phase activation
Phase I: Interim EV charging + paid parking on the lots during pre-development (~$8K-$20K/yr).
Phase II: 3-story walkup, 18-24 mixed-income units + ground-floor retail + rooftop solar + 6-10 EV stalls.
What's possible

Seven contiguous State-owned residential lots totaling 0.16 acres. The smallest urban infill in the portfolio — and the prototype. A 3-story walkup with 18–24 mixed-income units, ground-floor retail, rooftop solar, and 6–10 EV stalls — three policy wins (housing, infill, revenue) on the same footprint. Combined stabilized State revenue $48K–$131K/yr across three streams. Replicable to every small State parcel cluster in West Wilmington.

How the revenue works

The headline range ($48K–$131K/yr) is built from the revenue stream(s) below — each licensed to a private operator while the State keeps the land:

  • Solar. The State takes a 20–30% share of the developer-PPA energy value (~$81/MWh wholesale × ~14.3% Delaware capacity factor × the site’s MW). The developer finances, builds, and operates the array; the State collects a share and keeps the land.
  • Ground lease / redevelopment. Recurring ground rent on a developer-built project — the State leases the land, a developer builds vertical, and the State collects rent for the lease term without selling. Public ground rents run ~3–5% of land value, higher where vertical density (FAR) lifts the built value.
  • EV charging. A per-stall charging concession layered on the lease — small but recurring.
  • Parking control. District parking revenue and control — State-held parking lets the surrounding parcels redevelop without each having to solve for parking.

How we got the number. Each stream is a planning-level estimate from the PAW site brief applied to this parcel’s size, zoning, and corridor — not an executed lease. Because State parcels are tax-exempt, the county assigns no market land value, so both the land value (tile above) and the revenue are modeled — and firm up with a market / broker pull and DFM vetting.

What we surfaced
  • Valued and leased as a single 0.16-ac assemblage: planning-level land value $0.50M–$0.81M (mid $0.69M); recurring State revenue $48K–$131K/yr from one ground-lease + rooftop-solar + EV pathway across the seven lots.
  • Adjacent Housing Authority + affordable-housing context makes mixed-income the differentiator versus the BPG luxury comp.
  • Wilmington DDD rebate stack applies (City 2024: $24.5M → $436M private investment).
  • Replicable prototype: applied across 8–12 similar small State assemblages statewide, aggregate envelope $380K–$1.6M/yr + 200–400 workforce units at far lower entitlement risk than any single mega-site (brief v1.1).
Path forward
  • NCC parcel-viewer pull for all 7 parcel IDs, exact acreage, per-lot assessment.
  • Wetland screen across the 7 contiguous lots.
  • Quantify DDD developer rebate for the housing pro-forma.
Key risk
Treated as one 0.16-ac assemblage for both value and revenue, not seven separate lots. Parcel IDs and exact acreage still pending an NCC pull. The build/development value is illustrative, not underwritten; the wetland screen is not yet run on the assembled footprint.

Sources & methodology
Revenue methodology.

Energy basis: the State's 20-30% share is taken on the developer-PPA / wholesale value of generation (~$81/MWh, LevelTen PJM Q1 2026 proxy) - NOT the retail rate; Delaware PSC REPSA solicitation awards are the operative Delaware-specific comparable (not yet incorporated). Behind-the-meter avoided-cost (Delmarva commercial GS-T/GS-S tariff, verification pending) applies only to capacity sized to onsite State load.

Retail reference 16.5 c/kWh (EIA statewide average, Jan 2026) is a planning proxy and overstates commercial avoided-cost. Capacity factor 14.3% (NREL PVWatts: Wilmington TMY, 180 deg azimuth, 20 deg tilt, 14% losses, DC:AC 1.2).

SREC ~$30/MWh spot Yr 1-10 (SRECTrade 2026); SACP statutory ceiling $150/MWh (26 Del. C.

358(e)). Ground lease $600-$1,200/ac/yr Northeast benchmark (USDA NASS + NREL lease database verification pending).

State share 20-30% is an illustrative scenario (McAdams framework, Dec 2025), not a market-derived standard; FHWA Part 710 applies to ROW. All solar figures are planning-level estimates; methodology under active refinement against Delaware PSC-filed tariff and REPSA contract data.

Sources: PAW 514-520 W 8th brief v1.1; May 20, 2026 internal evaluation; DDD program (City of Wilmington 2024); BPG Justison Landing comp

Top: the site as it exists today. Bottom: an illustrative post-activation concept.

Phase activation
Phase I: Solar overlay 1.5-3.0 MW on rooftop + parking -> ~$30K-$91K/yr (planning-level, developer-PPA basis, 20-30% illustrative share), no operations impact.
Phase II: Preserve land-value optionality; structure Stage 1 PPA with an early-termination clause so it does not encumber Stage 2.
Phase III: If DMV operations consolidate or relocate, ground-lease or sale of the underlying campus land (16.91 ac; ~5 ac developable, Industrial-zoned) becomes the strategic asset - value pending appraisal.
What's possible

The site. a 16.91-acre State campus (~5 ac developed; remainder wetland/floodplain) at 501 S Heald Street, South Wilmington. The parcel is zoned Industrial. Currently the Wilmington DMV - fully occupied, no operational disruption available in the near term.

Phase I - Solar today (the no-regret play). Solar overlay on parking lot and rooftop, 1.5-3.0 MW. At a 14.3% capacity factor (NREL PVWatts, Wilmington TMY) and the State's 20-30% illustrative share of developer-PPA energy value (~$81/MWh PJM proxy, pending Delaware REPSA), this produces ~$30K-$91K/yr (planning-level). A behind-the-meter avoided-cost basis would run higher but applies only to capacity sized to onsite DMV load. No operations impact. Developer finances, builds, operates; the State licenses the surface and keeps the campus. Critical structuring point: Stage 1 solar should carry an early-termination/relocation clause so it does not become a 30-year encumbrance on Stage 2. A standard 30-year PPA without that clause forecloses the Phase II / III thesis.

Phase II / III - Land optionality preserved for later. Independent of Stage 1, the underlying land value materially exceeds the current administrative/operations value. South Wilmington industrial/commercial comparables suggest upside above the operational basis, but the land-value delta is not yet quantified and the comp basis must be industrial-zoned (pending appraisal). The Distributed Energy framework and the statewide DMV consolidation thesis both contemplate a future in which DMV operations consolidate or relocate. If that happens within a 10-year horizon, a Stage 2 ground lease or sale of the land becomes the strategic asset - materially larger than the Stage 1 solar value. The Stage 2 framework specifically contemplates a mixed public/private commercial redevelopment - the State retains land ownership through a structured ground lease; a private partner finances and operates the commercial mixed-use program; State operations relocate to a consolidated DMV footprint elsewhere in New Castle County.

What this means at the portfolio level. EN-1 is a strategic operational asset, not just a solar overlay. The thesis is solar today, land optionality preserved for later - both halves are part of the deliverable.

How the revenue works

The headline range (~$30K–$91K/yr (Stage 1 solar)) is built from the revenue stream(s) below — each licensed to a private operator while the State keeps the land:

  • Solar. The State takes a 20–30% share of the developer-PPA energy value (~$81/MWh wholesale × ~14.3% Delaware capacity factor × the site’s MW). The developer finances, builds, and operates the array; the State collects a share and keeps the land.
  • Ground lease / redevelopment. Recurring ground rent on a developer-built project — the State leases the land, a developer builds vertical, and the State collects rent for the lease term without selling. Public ground rents run ~3–5% of land value, higher where vertical density (FAR) lifts the built value.

How we got the number. Each stream is a planning-level estimate from the PAW site brief applied to this parcel’s size, zoning, and corridor — not an executed lease. Because State parcels are tax-exempt, the county assigns no market land value, so both the land value (tile above) and the revenue are modeled — and firm up with a market / broker pull and DFM vetting.

Phase activation

What's possible

The site. Ten contiguous State-owned parcels (C-2 zoning) along the SR-1 / US-13 cloverleaf in Camden, totaling 27.07 acres (GIS-verified). The highest-volume mixed commercial/residential corridor between Dover and the beaches.

What we surfaced - externally validated. The 2021 Delaware Statewide Truck Parking Study (CPCS / WILMAPCO / DelDOT) independently identified the US-13 / West Lebanon Rd / SR-10 intersection - the same cluster as these State-owned parcels - as a priority opportunity for truck parking capacity expansion. A state agency has already validated the demand at this location, and the State already controls the land. This is the strongest externally-validated revenue case in the portfolio. Additional demand validation: the Port of Wilmington Edgemoor container terminal expansion received Department of Army permits in April 2026. Construction of Phase I (400,000 TEU capacity, growing to 1.2 million TEU total) is now starting, with Phase I completion targeted for 2028. The expansion materially increases I-495 and US-13 truck traffic, making the documented absence of nearby truck parking an operationally acute constraint - not a hypothetical one.

Phase I - Cloverleaf stacked revenue + truck parking. The Cloverleaf framework runs four to five revenue streams on a single footprint: a solar canopy over surface parking, billboard slots oriented to both highway and corridor, cell-tower colocation on the highest pad, ground-leased commercial pads on the frontage, and - uniquely to Camden - a State-licensed truck staging operation. Conservative early-phase truck parking (30-50 trucks/night avg, Year 1-2) produces $50K-$185K/yr. Mature stabilized utilization (80-100 trucks/night, Year 3+) produces $140K-$525K/yr. Stacked with the other Cloverleaf streams, conceptual ceiling reaches $143K-$347K/yr per illustrative 8-acre subset (see Cloverleaf pathway).

Phase II - Hybrid commercial repositioning. Once the Phase I revenue streams are structured and operating, the 10-parcel set becomes a coordinated platform for hybrid retail/commercial development along the corridor. The corridor-commercialization typology applies here directly - replicable to every State-owned interchange parcel statewide.

What this means at the portfolio level. Camden is the corridor-commercialization demonstration AND the truck parking demonstration. Two co-located validated revenue cases on one cluster.

How the revenue works

The headline range ($180K–$450K/yr) is built from the revenue stream(s) below — each licensed to a private operator while the State keeps the land:

  • Solar. The State takes a 20–30% share of the developer-PPA energy value (~$81/MWh wholesale × ~14.3% Delaware capacity factor × the site’s MW). The developer finances, builds, and operates the array; the State collects a share and keeps the land.
  • Outdoor advertising & telecom. Annual license fees for billboard faces and cell / small-cell colocation on State frontage and ROW. Billboards need an FHWA / scenic-screen check; no State capital.
  • Truck parking / freight. Per-stall parking or build-to-suit logistics lease on freight-corridor land. Demand at this corridor was independently flagged by the 2021 WILMAPCO / DelDOT Statewide Truck Parking Study.
  • Parking control. District parking revenue and control — State-held parking lets the surrounding parcels redevelop without each having to solve for parking.

How we got the number. Each stream is a planning-level estimate from the PAW site brief applied to this parcel’s size, zoning, and corridor — not an executed lease. Because State parcels are tax-exempt, the county assigns no market land value, so both the land value (tile above) and the revenue are modeled — and firm up with a market / broker pull and DFM vetting.

Top: the site as it exists today. Bottom: an illustrative post-activation concept.

Phase activation
Phase II: Ground-lease activation (hospitality anchor + outparcel + solar overlay) -> stabilized $132K-$580K/yr (planning-level); gated by FY25 Bond Bill Section 46 (JCCI), salt-yard relocation funding ($3.7-5.3M), and a secured Tharros alternative.
What's possible

The site. 6.7 acres of State-owned C-1 General Commercial land at 18006 Coastal Highway, Lewes, at the Five Points node on DE Route 1 - one of Sussex County's highest-traffic commercial corridors. ~5 acres are net developable after wetland deduction. Former State Police Troop 7 (1983-2019; building demolished June 2024).

Current use - two active occupants. (1) A DelDOT salt-storage and brine operation for winter highway maintenance, and (2) Tharros Village, a Sussex County conditional-use seasonal encampment for residents experiencing homelessness. Activation has to address both: the salt operation is the structural keystone, Tharros is the political-acceptance gate.

The proposal - activate the land to generate recurring revenue. A ground-lease structure where a developer finances and builds and the State keeps the land and collects recurring rent. Three scenarios, each modeled with a stabilized case separate from an optimistic stacking ceiling: Scenario A (hospitality anchor + one outparcel) $310K-$580K/yr; Scenario B (mixed commercial + solar overlay) $220K-$420K/yr; Scenario C (full Cloverleaf stack, single-driveway constrained) stabilized $310K-$520K/yr. Across scenarios, stabilized recurring ground-lease income is $132K-$580K/yr (planning-level). A single shared DelDOT driveway (Corridor Capacity Preservation Program) limits how many revenue tiers can physically coexist - the stabilized case honors that constraint.

Revenue for housing. The activation is framed to support continued homeless-services investment, not displace it: revenue generated by the site can fund a documented alternative location for Tharros, and the recommended position is that no activation proceeds until a Tharros alternative is secured. This positions the State as investing in both economic activation and homeless services.

The gates. Two hard gates precede any RFP: (1) FY25 Bond Bill Section 46 requires Joint Committee on Capital Improvement co-chair approval before surplus/transfer/improvement; (2) the DelDOT salt operation must be relocated (Northeast DOT benchmarks put relocation at $3.7-5.3M) and funded outside the activation pro forma. The 30-year PV of mid-case rent (~$5.8M at a 2.5% public-sector real rate) roughly matches the relocation midpoint - so the economic case depends on a longer lease term, the higher revenue band, relocation funded separately, or an Option D partial activation on the unused remainder (~$80K-$160K/yr) that leaves the salt yard in place.

How the revenue works

The headline range ($132K–$580K/yr) is built from the revenue stream(s) below — each licensed to a private operator while the State keeps the land:

  • Solar. The State takes a 20–30% share of the developer-PPA energy value (~$81/MWh wholesale × ~14.3% Delaware capacity factor × the site’s MW). The developer finances, builds, and operates the array; the State collects a share and keeps the land.
  • Ground lease / redevelopment. Recurring ground rent on a developer-built project — the State leases the land, a developer builds vertical, and the State collects rent for the lease term without selling. Public ground rents run ~3–5% of land value, higher where vertical density (FAR) lifts the built value.

How we got the number. Each stream is a planning-level estimate from the PAW site brief applied to this parcel’s size, zoning, and corridor — not an executed lease. Because State parcels are tax-exempt, the county assigns no market land value, so both the land value (tile above) and the revenue are modeled — and firm up with a market / broker pull and DFM vetting.

Wilmington Cluster — District Infrastructure Platform (5 parcels)

The Wilmington Cluster — District Infrastructure Platform. Five State-owned parcels (Christina Garage, 168 Justison, Block 874, Block 869, Block 872) clustered across two blocks of downtown Wilmington. Read individually, each is a small redevelopment site. Read together, they are a publicly-controlled district infrastructure platform: parking inventory, operational campuses, TOD-staging parcels, and shared circulation under one owner. The State may already control enough parking and land in downtown Wilmington to influence redevelopment sequencing without directly becoming the developer. The cluster's principal asset class is optionality + control + sequencing, not direct lease revenue alone.

Mixed readiness — each parcel carries its own tier below (Block 874 is move-first; the garage and partnership parcels are active-operations).

What's possible

The anchor. The Christina Garage is an 800-stall State-owned garage with both excess parking capacity AND the structural authority to absorb the parking obligation of every adjacent cluster parcel (168 Justison, Block 874, Block 869, Block 872). This is the structural unlock for the entire Wilmington Cluster - because the parking sits on the State balance sheet, the surrounding parcels can be repositioned without each having to solve for parking.

Phase I - Near-term recurring revenue. A Stage 1 solar PPA on the garage roof - a typical 0.5-1.0 MW canopy producing an illustrative ~$10K-$30K/yr (planning-level, developer-PPA basis). EV charging stalls on the lower decks - licensed to a private operator producing $20K-$50K/yr per pad. Parking license revenue from absorbing adjacent-parcel parking obligations as redevelopment activates on Blocks 874, 869, 872.

Phase III - District infrastructure platform. As the cluster's TOD activations come online over time, the garage becomes the parking utility for the entire district. The State doesn't have to be the developer; it influences sequencing by controlling parking. This is the Wilmington-district-sequencing strategy made concrete.

What this means at the portfolio level. CL-1 is both a near-term revenue play AND the long-horizon district-infrastructure anchor. The two roles compound - Phase I revenue funds Phase III governance.

How the revenue works

The headline range (~$10K–$30K/yr (Stage 1 solar) + EV/parking) is built from the revenue stream(s) below — each licensed to a private operator while the State keeps the land:

  • Solar. The State takes a 20–30% share of the developer-PPA energy value (~$81/MWh wholesale × ~14.3% Delaware capacity factor × the site’s MW). The developer finances, builds, and operates the array; the State collects a share and keeps the land.
  • Ground lease / redevelopment. Recurring ground rent on a developer-built project — the State leases the land, a developer builds vertical, and the State collects rent for the lease term without selling. Public ground rents run ~3–5% of land value, higher where vertical density (FAR) lifts the built value.
  • EV charging. A per-stall charging concession layered on the lease — small but recurring.
  • Parking control. District parking revenue and control — State-held parking lets the surrounding parcels redevelop without each having to solve for parking.

How we got the number. Each stream is a planning-level estimate from the PAW site brief applied to this parcel’s size, zoning, and corridor — not an executed lease. Because State parcels are tax-exempt, the county assigns no market land value, so both the land value (tile above) and the revenue are modeled — and firm up with a market / broker pull and DFM vetting.

Phase activation
Phase I: Stage 1 solar canopy on 0.52 ac of surface parking + EV charging. ▲ Standalone-capable

What's possible

The site. Two State parcels on Block 874 (117 MLK + 114 W 2nd), 0.52 acres of currently-surface-parking land in OZ Tract 10003001902. Proof-of-concept for solar canopy deployment is one block away at the DelTech 206 W Second deployed deck.

Phase I - Near-term solar + EV. With the Christina Garage carrying the parking obligation, Block 874 doesn't need to solve for parking. The surface can host a solar canopy + EV charging in the near term - interim revenue while the redevelopment moment matures.

Phase II - TOD activation when the moment arrives. ~14,000 sf vertical commercial at C-3 FAR 6 with no parking minimum (capacity, not a revenue claim). 4-7 story mixed-use TOD in OZ Tract 10003001902 with QOZ benefits stacked. The State doesn't pick the redevelopment moment now; it captures interim revenue from solar/EV while preserving the long-term mid-rise OZ-stacked optionality.

The phasing IS the strategy. Block 874 demonstrates the cluster's two-speed structure: passive ground revenue today, vertical redevelopment optionality intact.

How the revenue works

The headline range (Interim solar/EV + Phase II TOD) is built from the revenue stream(s) below — each licensed to a private operator while the State keeps the land:

  • Solar. The State takes a 20–30% share of the developer-PPA energy value (~$81/MWh wholesale × ~14.3% Delaware capacity factor × the site’s MW). The developer finances, builds, and operates the array; the State collects a share and keeps the land.
  • Ground lease / redevelopment. Recurring ground rent on a developer-built project — the State leases the land, a developer builds vertical, and the State collects rent for the lease term without selling. Public ground rents run ~3–5% of land value, higher where vertical density (FAR) lifts the built value.
  • EV charging. A per-stall charging concession layered on the lease — small but recurring.

How we got the number. Each stream is a planning-level estimate from the PAW site brief applied to this parcel’s size, zoning, and corridor — not an executed lease. Because State parcels are tax-exempt, the county assigns no market land value, so both the land value (tile above) and the revenue are modeled — and firm up with a market / broker pull and DFM vetting.

What's possible

The site. A triangular State parcel pressed against the rail edge - geometry that limits standalone redevelopment but maximizes its value as district circulation, utility siting, and assemblage land. Adjacent to BPG's live Justison Landing project (164 units, $56.5M, ~$349/sf - Fall 2026).

Phase I - Quiet revenue, quiet assembly. Surface staging during BPG construction. Utility / telecom siting agreements. Small-cell colocation. Modest interim revenue while the parcel's strategic role develops. Adjacent State parking deck capacity (Christina Garage, CL-1) provides shared parking support for any near-term Justison activation - the cluster's parking-on-balance-sheet structure means 168 Justison does not need to solve for parking independently.

Phase II / III - Assemblage land for the first cluster redevelopment. Within the cluster's parking-on-balance-sheet structure (Christina Garage carrying the parking obligation), 168 Justison becomes the staging parcel for whichever Block 874 or Block 869 redevelopment moves first. The geometry that limits standalone use becomes an asset in assemblage.

What this means at the portfolio level. CL-2 is a connector parcel, not a standalone revenue parcel. Its value is in district sequencing - a different kind of value than the rest of the portfolio carries, and one that justifies its inclusion at lower individual revenue confidence.

Section 3

Activation Systems & Revenue Pathways

The Evidence Base

The State's advantage is not development. It is land control and licensing leverage.

Six activation systems turn underused public land into recurring revenue — distributed energy, freight & logistics, corridor commercialization, TOD & downtown redevelopment, passive infrastructure, and parking/operations consolidation. Across all of them the model is the same: the State licenses the parcel, a private operator finances and builds and operates, and the State collects the recurring stream and keeps the land. No upfront capital, no operational risk, no tax increase. Peer references — Maryland DOT, MassDOT, and Cook County — have already converted analogous assets using this structure.

Each system below carries its Delaware policy context, benchmark rates, comparable programs, the sites where it applies, and sourced citations. These establish defensible, market-supported ranges — not parcel-level guarantees. Every figure traces to a publicly verified source (see Methodology & Citations).

⚠ Read before any stacked example. Illustrative stacked scenarios are conceptual. They are not additive assumptions guaranteed to coexist on any single parcel. Each system has its own permitting, spacing, federal-aid, and feasibility constraints. Treat stacked totals as an upper-bound concept, not a planning figure.
01
MDOT · MassDOT · The Ray · NEVI

Distributed Energy

PLANNING-LEVEL — inputs under validation (PSC tariff / REPSA pending)Phase IPhase II overlaySolarEV Charging

Highest-volume system in the portfolio. Solar on roofs, parking canopies, and highway ROW (344 MW / 2,626 ac of DelDOT ROW identified statewide), plus EV charging on State frontage adjacent to NEVI corridors.

At a glance

Solar. Highway interchanges, surface parking, and large campus rooftops are viable solar surfaces. A developer finances, builds, and operates under a PPA or ground lease; the State licenses the surface and takes a share of value. Maryland DOT executed this exact model in a $50M portfolio (March 2026). The Ray Highway Geospatial Solutions team independently identified 2,626 acres of viable DelDOT ROW (~344 MW) statewide.

EV charging. Delaware has $17.6M in committed federal NEVI funding. State-owned parcels adjacent to NEVI corridors can capture revenue by licensing charging sites to private operators — revenue currently left to private landowners (all 12 NEVI Round 1 awards went to private sites).

⚠ Planning-level methodology under active refinement. The State's 20–30% share is taken on the developer-PPA / wholesale value of generation, not the retail rate. Behind-the-meter avoided-cost applies only to capacity sized to onsite State load. Figures pending validation against Delaware PSC-filed Delmarva tariffs and REPSA contract awards.
Delaware policy context
  • Renewable Portfolio Standard raised to 40% by 2035 — sustained developer demand.
  • Solar carve-out 3.5% of total electricity for the 2025–2026 energy year.
  • Solar Alternative Compliance Payment $150/MWh (26 Del. C. §358(e)) — statutory ceiling supporting SREC value; SREC spot ~$30/MWh in years 1–10.
  • DE retail rate 16.5 ¢/kWh (EIA statewide avg, Jan 2026) — planning proxy only; the operative avoided-cost for State commercial facilities is the Delmarva GS-T/GS-S tariff (lower), verification pending.
  • Distributed Energy framework (Dec 22, 2025) establishes a 20–30% State share on developer-operated installations.
  • EV: NEVI Round 1 (12 corridor awards) + DNREC Clean Transportation rebates up to 90% through Apr 30, 2026.

Ground lease — premium / stacked$1,500–$3,500/ac/yrSubstation adjacency, canopy, or premium frontage

Comparable programs
  • Maryland DOT — $50M solar portfolio via the Strategic Energy Investment Fund ($0.5M FY26 + $40M FY27 + $9.5M FY28); 115 acres; ~35 MW; ~20% of MDOT's own electricity. MDOT leases land; developer finances/operates; developer captures federal tax incentives. Direct replicable model.
  • MassDOT — same structure on highway ROW (Renewable Energy Projects).
  • Camden NEVI award — went to a private gas station on US-13; State-owned C-2 parcels on the same corridor are unoccupied. Demand validated; State not yet participating as host. Pattern holds across all 12 Round 1 sites.

WILMAPCO 2021 · DelDOT FY2026 · Jason's Law

Freight & Logistics

HIGHEST DELAWARE-SPECIFIC EVIDENCEPhase IPhase IITruck Parking

The single strongest externally-validated system: truck parking and port staging on State land adjacent to the interstate freight network — demand documented by a State-commissioned study, supply confirmed deficient.

At a glance

A 2021 State-commissioned WILMAPCO/DelDOT study independently identified specific State-owned locations as deficient in truck parking. An active FY2025/2026 DelDOT capital request seeks funding for the same facilities, and FHWA Jason's Law flags the I-95 corridor as a national shortage area. The Camden cluster named in the 2021 study is the same cluster as the State-owned C-2 parcels on the SA-2 card. A state agency has validated the demand; the State already controls the land. (Jason's Law survey: 11,696 drivers; 98% report problems finding safe parking, 75% at least weekly; 79% of truck-stop operators do not plan expansion.)

Delaware policy context

Delaware Statewide Truck Parking Study (CPCS / WILMAPCO / DelDOT, Sept 2021). Statewide existing supply: 12 locations / 337 spaces; 32 undesignated tractor-trailer clusters identified as deficient. Five priority locations:

  1. Port Area Truck Parking Facility (near Port of Wilmington)
  2. Edgemoor site (adjacent to the Port)
  3. US-13 / Bear Rd / Hamburg Rd (NCC)
  4. US-13 / West Lebanon Rd / SR-10 (Camden — overlaps SA-2)
  5. SR-1 / Milford Bypass
  • FY2026 DelDOT Capital Budget — active unfunded truck-parking request.
  • Port of Wilmington Edgemoor expansion (Army permits April 2026; Phase I to 1.2M TEU, 2028) makes nearby parking acute.

03
Cook County Cloverleaf · CGI Phase 3

Corridor Commercialization

INTEGRATION PATTERNPhase IPhase IICloverleaf stacking

Commercial ground leases on high-traffic State frontage — and the Cloverleaf model that stacks several revenue streams on one interchange footprint so a single parcel set earns like many.

At a glance

As-of-right or conditional-use commercial zoning plus Title 29 disposition lets the State ground-lease corridor frontage: the developer builds and operates, the State keeps the land and collects rent. The Cloverleaf is the integration move — solar canopy + billboard + cell colocation + ground-leased pads + (at Camden) truck staging on one footprint. Demonstrated on Cook County interchange parcels and codified in the CGI Phase 3 Brief (May 8, 2026).

Wilmington DDD · BPG Justison · Biden Station

TOD & Downtown Redevelopment

MEDIUM — live local comps; entitlement-dependentPhase IIPhase IIIGround Lease + HousingOpportunity Zone

Transit- and downtown-anchored mixed-use on State parcels inside established incentive districts — ground lease + housing/commercial build, with solar and EV overlays adding recurring tiers.

At a glance

State parcels inside Wilmington's Downtown Development District (and the Wilmington Cluster) support transit-oriented, mixed-use redevelopment: the State ground-leases the land, a developer builds vertical (housing + ground-floor commercial), and the City DDD rebate plus Opportunity-Zone treatment close the pro-forma. The State keeps the land and collects recurring rent while adding housing supply downtown. Solar on common areas and an EV podium layer additional recurring tiers on the same footprint.

Delaware policy context
  • Wilmington Downtown Development District (DDD) — City rebate framework stacked on a State ground lease.
  • Opportunity Zone overlay where tracts qualify — eligible, subject to 2027 re-designation (OZ 1.0 deferral ends 12/31/2026).
  • Wilmington zoning (C-3 Central Retail FAR 6; downtown residential districts) supports mid-rise vertical with reduced parking minimums — confirm parameters against Wilmington Code Ch. 48 before any capacity claim.
  • Ground lease + housing build; EV-charging and rooftop solar overlays add recurring tiers.

05
DivCom · Crown Castle · FHWA 23 CFR 750

Passive Infrastructure Revenue

MIXED — telecom HIGH; billboards CONDITIONALPhase ITelecomOutdoor Advertising

Cell-tower and small-cell licensing on existing State infrastructure (DivCom), plus billboard/digital-signage on highway frontage — recurring lease income, no State capital. Telecom is the strong, ready half; billboards are conditional upside.

At a glance

Telecom (strong). Delaware already operates DivCom — a statewide 800 MHz trunked-radio system with towers on State-controlled sites across all three counties. Licensing commercial carrier colocation on existing towers generates revenue from infrastructure the State already owns. A single DivCom data request (site count, colocation status, lease terms) is a zero-cost first step.

Outdoor advertising (conditional). Highway-adjacent frontage can host billboards, but federal-aid ROW, the Highway Beautification Act, scenic-corridor designations, and safety-ramp spacing can disqualify any given parcel. Treat as conditional upside — every site needs a federal-aid screen with DelDOT before any billboard line item is presented.

Delaware policy context
  • DivCom (Division of Communications) operates the State's 800 MHz Digital Trunked Radio System; towers on State land across all agencies, fire, EMS.
  • Billboards on federally-funded ROW require FHWA coordination under 23 CFR Part 750 + the Highway Beautification Act; landowner ground rent typically 15–20% of gross.
  • Required per-parcel billboard screen: federal-aid ROW determination, scenic/Beautification review, safety-ramp spacing, local sign ordinance.

Parking, Operations & Consolidation

HIGH — avoided-cost, identifiedPhase IPhase IIIParking controlLease consolidation

State control of parking and operations campuses, consolidated to free underused land and cut lease cost. This is avoided cost that reads straight to the budget — and the structural unlock for the Wilmington Cluster.

At a glance

Two moves. Parking control: the Christina Garage absorbs the parking obligation of every adjacent Wilmington Cluster parcel, so the surrounding blocks can be repositioned without each solving for parking — the State influences district sequencing by controlling the parking utility. Lease consolidation: renegotiating pre-COVID State leases at market and consolidating operations campuses frees land and cuts cost.

Note: consolidation savings are avoided cost, a separate budget line from State-land revenue — not counted in the portfolio revenue headline.

  • Parking control is the structural unlock for the Wilmington Cluster (Christina Garage carries cluster parking on the State balance sheet).
  • Campus consolidation via Title 29 surplus where operations relocate (e.g., DMV / Dover optionality).

Section 4

Methodology & Citations

Every dollar figure on the Atlas can be reproduced from a public data source and a stated formula. Where State-internal documents or working assumptions are used, they are flagged separately. This is screening-level methodology; formal RFP pricing requires independent appraisal, parking study, and developer market test.

A. Land valuation

The Atlas does not use parcel assessments as land comps — assessments are administrative, not market transactions. Four methods, in order of preference:

Method 1 — CPI-adjusted prior arms-length acquisition.
Land Value (today) = Prior Acquisition Price × (CPI today ÷ CPI at acquisition). Source: BLS CPI-U Northeast Urban [1]. Use when a clean prior arms-length acquisition of the exact parcel exists; treat as a floor.
Method 2 — Comparable land-only transactions.
Source: county Recorders of Deeds + LoopNet [2][3][4][5]. Use when 2–3 recent land-only sales exist within ½ mile, same zoning. Discard sales that include vertical improvements.
Method 3 — Land residual (sanity check).
Land Value = (Stabilized NOI ÷ Cap Rate) − Vertical Build Cost. Cap rates / build costs from Cushman & Wakefield Mid-Atlantic Q1 2026 and RSMeans 2026 [6][7]. Triangulation only — no published Atlas figure is derived from this method; cap-rate/build-cost sources [6][7] apply only if a residual check is run.
Method 4 — Indicative range pending appraisal. Wilmington downtown commercial benchmark for a half-acre parcel: $5M low / $8–12M mid / $15M+ high. Planning-level placeholder, not an appraisal.

B. Ground rent

Annual Ground Rent = Land Fee-Simple Value × Ground Rent %.

Public-sector ground rent is 3% conservative / 4% mid / 5% high of fee-simple land value. The Atlas does not use 5–8% references — those apply to private-to-private deals in Manhattan, San Francisco, and downtown DC, not Delaware public-sector dispositions. Benchmark set: Battery Park City Authority [8]; Boston Planning & Development Agency [9]; GSA Public Buildings Service [10].

C. Solar revenue

Two formulas depending on whether the system serves on-site State load (behind-the-meter) or exports to grid (wholesale PPA).

Behind-the-meter (avoided cost) — applies only to capacity sized to onsite State load: Annual State Revenue = MW × 1,250 kWh/kW-yr × rate × State Share %. Retail proxy $0.165/kWh (EIA statewide avg, Jan 2026 [12]) overstates commercial avoided-cost; the operative figure is the Delmarva GS-T/GS-S commercial tariff (~$0.10–0.13, verification pending). CF 14.3% = NREL PVWatts (Wilmington TMY; 180° azimuth; 20° tilt; 14% losses; DC:AC 1.2) [11]; State Share 20–30% illustrative (McAdams framework, Dec 2025 — internal).

Worked (corrected, developer-PPA basis) — EN-1 Wilmington DMV (1.5–3.0 MW): low 1.5 × 1,250 × $0.081 × 20% = $30,375/yr; high 3.0 × 1,250 × $0.081 × 30% = $91,125/yr. Planning-level (developer-PPA basis).

Developer-PPA / export (the primary basis for developer-financed generation): Annual State Revenue = MW × 1,250 kWh/kW-yr × $0.081/kWh × State Share %.
~$81/MWh = LevelTen PJM solar PPA index (2025) [13]. ⚠ Delaware PSC REPSA solicitation awards are the operative Delaware-specific comparable — not yet incorporated.

Worked — EN-3 Ray ROW (6.95 MW): low = $112,000/yr; high = $168,000/yr.

D. Discount rate & PV factors

The Atlas uses a 2.5% real discount rate (OMB Circular A-94 App. C [14]). PV of Annual Cash Flow = Annual Revenue × PV Factor.

TermUse casePV factor @ 2.5% real
30-yrStandard structured ground lease initial term20.93
65-yrLayered ground lease with extension options31.96

Worked: 30-yr PV of $200K/yr = $200K × 20.93 = $4.19M.

E. Cloverleaf stacked revenue

Total Annual Cloverleaf Revenue = Σ (component revenue).

ComponentFormulaSource
Solar canopySee Section CEIA / LevelTen / NREL
Billboard (per face)$30K–$60K/yrOutfront + Lamar 10-Ks 2026 [15]
Cell tower (per carrier)$24K–$72K/yrAmerican Tower + Crown Castle 10-Ks 2026 [16]

Worked — Camden 1-acre illustrative: 1 MW solar × $195K × 25% = $49K; 2 billboard faces × $45K = $90K; 1 monopole × 3 carriers × $48K = $144K; 1 pad ($2M × 4%) = $80K. Total ≈ $363K/yr (illustrative).

G. Worked examples — three sites end-to-end

SA-1 Salt Yard ground lease: appraisal $4.4M–$5.1M; public-sector ground rent 3–5% (Hilton Head / Cape May comps). Stabilized across scenarios $132K–$580K/yr (hospitality anchor + outparcel + solar overlay; single-driveway constrained). 30-yr PV at $275K mid ≈ $5.8M at 2.5% real — roughly matching the $4.5M salt-relocation midpoint, so the case needs a longer term, the higher band, or relocation funded separately. Tharros Village is the seasonal homeless encampment on site (a political gate), not a revenue layer.
EN-1 Wilmington DMV solar (corrected): 1.5–3.0 MW; CF 14.3%; developer-PPA $0.081; State share 20–30% → ~$30K–$91K/yr (planning-level). Behind-the-meter avoided-cost (onsite load only) would run higher, pending Delmarva commercial-tariff verification.
CL-1 Christina Garage land (CPI sanity check): the 2004 acquisition ($2,460,000), CPI-adjusted on the BLS Northeast-Urban CPI-U index, yields a low-single-digit-$M floor (exact index factor pending the current BLS release — not asserted here). Because Wilmington downtown commercial land has materially outpaced general CPI, the defensible mid-range for the Christina Garage land is $8M–$12M per Method 4 (Wilmington downtown benchmark).

J. Reproducibility standard

Every dollar range on this Atlas can be reproduced by: (1) identifying which formula (Sections A–F) applies, (2) pulling the inputs from the cited public source (Section H), (3) running the math. If a reader finds a number that cannot be reproduced from this page, that is a defect — flag it and we will reconcile.

Scope note. This page documents screening-level methodology. It does not substitute for formal appraisal, parking study, environmental review, title search, or developer market test. All ranges are planning-level estimates and should be validated before any RFP, disposition, or capital commitment. The Christina Garage CPI example states the method and a Method-4 range rather than a single unverified CPI factor; the land-residual (Method 3) is included for completeness only and drives no published figure.

Aggregate portfolio headline — $5–15M/yr (methodology)

Bottoms-up build across three layers: (1) the 14 priority projects at stabilized operations ($1.2M–$4.4M/yr); (2) four additional WILMAPCO-identified truck-parking candidate sites at mature stabilized utilization ($0.2M–$2.1M/yr); and (3) statewide pipeline scale-up across DelDOT ROW solar (~337 MW remaining beyond the Ray sites at PPA × State share), DivCom commercial colocation expansion (50–100 implementable sites), and corridor commercial ground leases outside the priority portfolio ($3.5M–$8M/yr).

Solar inputs: EIA Electric Power Monthly Jan 2026 retail rate (16.5 ¢/kWh) for on-State-campus systems; LevelTen Q1 2026 PJM PPA ($64.49/MWh) for off-campus / grid-export; NREL PVWatts capacity factor 14.3% (1,250 kWh/kW-yr); McAdams Distributed Energy memo (Dec 22, 2025) State share 20–30%. Truck parking: 2021 WILMAPCO/DelDOT Statewide Truck Parking Study priority locations; mature stabilized utilization (80–100 trucks/night, Year 3+) per FHWA Jason’s Law and the Cook County Cloverleaf comparable.

Excluded from this headline: conditional billboard revenue (requires federal-aid + scenic + safety screens per parcel); campus-consolidation cost-avoidance (~$2.46M/yr, a separate P&L line from State-land revenue); and full statewide pipeline at upper-bound concurrent execution.

Illustrative. Pathway-level estimates assume independent execution and are not additive guarantees. Final values depend on permitting, market sounding, federal screens, operator agreements, and parcel-level appraisal. The range narrows or widens with completion of diligence on each priority project.
